utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-9-PT, the Prosecutor against Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, Stevan Todorovic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Nancy Paterson representing the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, Deyan Brashich, representing the Todorovic Defence. I'm joined today by my co-counsel Mr. Nikola Kostich of the Wisconsin and Illinois bars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to make sure that the accused is hearing the proceedings in a language that he understands. Mr. Todorovic. THE ACCUSED TODOROVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. There is before a Trial Chamber a motion submitted jointly by the Prosecution and the Defence reflecting an agreement whereby the accused, Stevan Todorovic, will plead guilty to Count 1 of the indictment on the understanding that all the specific charges in the remaining counts are encompassed by the general charge of persecution, a crime against humanity. The agreement also provides that the accused will withdraw all motions pending before the Trial Chamber relating to an evidentiary hearing regarding the circumstances of his arrest and his request for judicial assistance. Specifically, he will withdraw the allegations that his arrest was unlawful and that SFOR or NATO was involved in any unlawful activity in relation to his arrest. On two previous occasions in the history of the Tribunal, guilty pleas have been made by accused persons. On the first occasion, the plea was made at initial appearance, and in the second, shortly after Initial Appearance. But significantly, on both occasions, the plea was heard by a fully constituted Trial Chamber. What distinguishes this case from those is that this plea is being taken about two years after initial appearance, albeit before the commencement of trial and, secondly, by a single judge. Rule 62 bis governs the taking of guilty pleas in accordance with Rule 62(vi) which deals with pleas of guilty on initial appearance. However Rule 62 bis also relates to a change of a plea to guilty after initial appearance and that is the present situation. While the Rule is clear that it is a Trial Chamber that enters a finding of guilt based upon a guilty plea and is also clear as to the matters in respect of which such a Chamber must be satisfied before it enters a finding of guilt based upon such a plea, it is silent as to what governs the situation in which the plea of guilty is made before a single Judge or a Chamber not fully constituted. What is certain, however, is that when the plea is taken by a single Judge or a Chamber not fully constituted, it must be referred to the Trial Chamber for it to be satisfied as to the matters set out in Rule 62 bis before it enters a finding of guilt. Those matters include the voluntariness of the plea and that the plea is informed. If there is a lacuna in the Rules, there is none in the law for it would be unsafe and inconsistent with the rights of the accused for any judicial body to receive and record a plea of guilty without being satisfied as to certain matters that relate to the rights of the accused under customary international law. And this, notwithstanding that the Trial Chamber to which the plea must be referred must also be satisfied about the same matters if he is to enter a finding of guilt. Notwithstanding the fact, therefore, that the plea will have to be referred to the Trial Chamber, I have a duty to be satisfied as to certain matters including, in particular, the voluntariness of the plea and that the accused fully understands the plea and its consequences. In considering a plea of guilty, the Tribunal must take into account the interests of the accused as they are reflected in his fundamental rights and also, importantly, international public interest. The procedure that we will follow for this plea in relation to the joint motion is that I'll call firstly on the Prosecutor to introduce the motion and thereafter the Defence. Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As you have stated, on 29 November 2000, the Office of the Prosecutor and the representatives for Mr. Todorovic, Mr. Brashich and Mr. Kostich filed a joint motion before this court bringing to your attention a written plea agreement that had been negotiated and agreed to between Mr. Todorovic and the Office of the Prosecutor. Pursuant to that agreement, as you have said, Mr. Brashich is prepared to withdraw the motions currently pending before this Chamber and which are the matter currently before the Appeals Chamber. In addition, pursuant to that agreement, the Office of the Prosecutor is recommending to the Trial Chamber that the accused be allowed to plead guilty only to count 1 of the indictment, charging persecutions. I am not prepared to provide any further details in public of the plea agreement other than to state that the Prosecutor and the accused have agreed that if the accused complies fully with all aspects of the plea agreement, the Office of the Prosecutor will recommend to the Trial Chamber that they impose a sentence of not less than 5 years and not more than 12 years. Having said that, however, it is also understood by the accused and the Office of the Prosecutor that on the day of sentence, both the Prosecutor and the accused are free to argue for a particular period of incarceration within that range of 5 to 12 years. Turning now to the case against Mr. Todorovic. If this case were to go to trial, the Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to prove beyond a reasonable doubt, with regard to count 1, persecutions, a crime against humanity, that Stevan Todorovic willingly participated in an armed conflict, during which he knowingly committed acts which were part of a widespread or systemic attack against the population and that Stevan Todorovic knew his acts were part of the broader context of such an attack. The Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to call witnesses and to introduce documentary evidence and other forms of evidence that would prove beyond a reasonable doubt that from 17 April 1992 through at least 31 December 1993, Stevan Todorovic and others planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted certain acts of persecution against the Bosnian Croat, Bosnian Muslim, and other non-Serb civilians throughout the municipality of Bosanski Samac and elsewhere in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that Stevan Todorovic participated in these acts of persecution on political, racial, and religious grounds. More specifically, the Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Stevan Todorovic, along with other men, wilfully beat and kicked Anto Brandic, also known as Antesa, on 29 July 1992 in the Bosanski Samac police station and thereby caused the death of Anto Brandic. Furthermore, the Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to prove that Stevan Todorovic intended to cause the death of Anto Brandic and that Anto Brandic was a person who was not taking active part in the hostilities. The Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to prove that Stevan Todorovic wilfully ordered six men, whose names will not be publicly disclosed, to perform the sexual act of fellatio on each other at the police station in Bosanski Samac on three different occasions in May and June of 1992. The Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to prove that Stevan Todorovic wilfully beat Enver Ibralic, Hasan Jasarevic, Omer Nalic and Father Jozo Puskaric on about 29 July, 1992 in the hallway of the police building in Bosanski Samac; that Stevan Todorovic beat Silvester Antunovic on about 15 July 1992 in the gymnasium of the Bosanski Samac primary school and beat Hasan Bicic, Kemal Bobic, Hasan Ceribasic, Abdulah Drljacic, Zlatko Dubric, Roko Jelavic and Hasan Subasic on several occasions between 17 April 1992 and 21 November 1992 in the primary school, the secondary school, and the Territorial Defence building in Bosanski Samac, and that all of the victims suffered significant physical and mental injuries as a result of the beatings. The Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to prove that Stevan Todorovic wilfully ordered and committed the unlawful detention and confinement of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims, and other non-Serb civilians under inhumane conditions on political, racial, or religious grounds and not for their protection and safety. The Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to prove that Stevan Todorovic wilfully ordered and committed the cruel and inhumane treatment of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims, and other non-Serb civilians by means of beatings, torture, forced labour assignments, and confinement under inhumane conditions, and that the inhumane treatment caused great suffering or serious injury to body or to the mental or physical health of the victims. The Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to prove that Stevan Todorovic ordered other men over whom he had superior responsibility to torture Omer Nalic on about 19 June 1992 at the Bosanski Samac primary school and in so doing knowingly committed and aided and abetted the commission of the crime of torture. The evidence would also have shown that severe mental and physical pain or suffering was inflicted on Omer Nalic as a result of this treatment. Furthermore, the Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to prove that the acts of torture were committed by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of Stevan Todorovic, who was an official or a person acting in an official capacity for one or more of the following purposes: to obtain information or a confession from the victim or a third person; to punish the victim for an act the victim or a third person committed or was suspected of having committed; to intimidate or coerce the victim or a third person or for any reason based upon discrimination of any kind. Additionally, with respect to the underlying offence of torture, the Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to prove that Stevan Todorovic is criminally responsible as a superior for the acts of his subordinates, pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal, because he knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit the crime of torture, and he failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures prevent to such acts or punish the perpetrators thereof. The Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to prove that Stevan Todorovic ordered and participated in the interrogation of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims, and other non-Serb civilians --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please. Could the counsel slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, you are being asked to slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I'm trying very hard to speak slowly, Your Honour, but I'll try harder. The Office of the Prosecutor was also prepared to prove that Stevan Todorovic wilfully ordered and participated in the deportation, forcible transfer, and expulsion of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims, and other non-Serb civilians, including women, children, and the elderly, from their homes and villages by force, intimidation and coercion. The Office of the Prosecutor was prepared to prove that Stevan Todorovic issued orders and directives which violated the rights of the Bosnian Croat, Bosnian Muslim, and other non-Serb civilians to equal treatment under the law and infringed upon their enjoyment of basic and fundamental rights. The Office of the Prosecutor has agreed to allow the accused to plead to only the first count of the indictment because the charge of persecutions by its nature also encompasses all the allegations detailed in counts 2 to 27 of the indictment. Specifically, by pleading guilty to the charge of persecutions, the Office of the Prosecutor is satisfied that Stevan Todorovic has, in essence, acknowledged that he, along with other men, beat and kicked Anto Brandic, also known as Antesa, and thereby caused his death; that he ordered six men to perform sexual acts on each other at the police station in Bosanski Samac; that he beat Enver Ibralic, Hasan Jasarevic, Omer Nalic, Father Jozo Puskaric, Silvester Antunovic, Hasan Bicic, Kemal Bobic, Hasan Ceribasic, Abdulah Drljacic, Zlatko Dubric, Roko Jelavic, and Hasan Subasic in the primary school, the secondary school, and the Territorial Defence building in Bosanski Samac; that he ordered and committed the unlawful detention and confinement of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims and other non-Serb civilians under inhumane conditions; that he ordered and committed the cruel and inhumane treatment of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims, and other non-Serb civilians; that he ordered other men to torture Omer Nalic at the Bosanski Samac primary school; that he ordered and participated in the interrogation of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims, and other non-Serb civilians and forced them to sign false and coerced statements; that he ordered and participated in the deportation, forcible transfer, and expulsion of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims, and other non-Serb civilians from their homes and villages; and that he issued orders and directives which violated the rights of the Bosnian Croat, Bosnian Muslim, and other non-Serb civilians to equal treatment under the law and infringed upon their enjoyment of basic and fundamental human rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Paterson. Ms. Paterson, there are two matters that I'd like to raise with you and they have to do with the correspondence between counts 2 to 26 and count 1 to which the plea of guilty will relate as well as the correspondence between the factual basis as set out in the agreement and indeed as you have just set it out and count one. The first matter is whereas paragraph (b) of count 1 charges the accused with murders, counts 4, 5, and 6 of the indictment relate to one specific victim and indeed you have confirmed that in the factual basis set out in the agreement and in the statement that you just made. What I would like to find out is if the matter were to go to trial, would the Prosecution be adducing evidence of more than one murder as is alleged in paragraph 34(b) of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the testimony at trial would have shown that Mr. Todorovic was aware that more than one person was murdered in the police station and in the camps that were set up in Bosanski Samac; however, we were prepared only to prove one count of murder against Mr. Todorovic involving this one victim that I have mentioned, Mr. Brandic. So it would be incorrect to say that we were prepared to prove that Mr. Todorovic was responsible for more than one murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You would only adduce evidence as to the one murder.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Anto Brandic. The second matter is -- has to do with the question of correspondence. Under paragraph 28 of the general allegations in the indictment, superior responsibility as set out in Article 7(3) of the Statute would apply to all the charges. However, paragraphs 2(e) and 3(f) of the agreement appear to confine that responsibility to the single charge of torture and you have just confirmed that in the statement that you made. So the question is similar to the one which I asked first, that is, were the case to go to trial, would you be adducing evidence that would show the superior responsibility of the accused in respect of other charges, that is, charges other than torture?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: In answer to your question, no. If this case were to go to trial, we would only be adducing evidence that Mr. Todorovic could be held responsible under 7(3) for that one count of torture against Omer Nalic. On all the other counts, he would be responsible only under Article 7(1) for individual responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for the clarification. Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I join with Ms. Paterson in the motion that the plea agreement be accepted and I am mindful of the fact that only a full Chamber can accept my client's plea. I have heard the representations made by Ms. Paterson were this matter to go to trial, what the Prosecutor would have proven. I am also mindful of this Chamber's decision and order of October 18, 2000. If this case proceeded further, the Defence would have relied on the presumption of innocence, and would this case have gone further and proceeded further to trial, the Defence would have requested that the Court take judicial notice of a finding of guilt rendered yesterday by the district court at Uzice finding a number of individuals guilty of the kidnapping and the abduction of my client. Had this matter proceeded further, the Defence would have relied on evidence and brought documentary evidence and adduced oral and other proofs showing that my client's abduction and seizure violated a number of his rights. I note, for the record, that this Court, I believe, in its decision, has guarded my client's rights and that individuals other than those that were convicted and sentenced to terms of incarceration in the -- by the district court in Uzice -- and I've lost my train of thought at this point, Your Honour -- that other individuals had participated in this abduction and most probably paid for such abduction. However, Your Honour, we are here under a negotiated plea agreement that the Prosecutor has entered with the Defence and for the purposes of the plea agreement, it is correct that one of the points in the agreement, as Ms. Paterson has pointed out is, notwithstanding the representations which I have just made as to my client's abduction and of the individuals involved in such abduction, that as a result of a plea agreement, the Defence is willing under paragraph 8 of the agreement, for the purposes of the plea agreement only, to withdraw my request for judicial assistance and to withdraw that particular application and to make, for the purposes of this plea agreement, a representation that we will not seek the disclosure and reports and documents from SFOR and NATO and that the Defence request that General Sinseki require to provide testimony in any evidentiary hearings be also withdrawn. For the purposes of the plea bargain agreement, the Defence withdraws its allegations that his arrest was unlawful and that SFOR or NATO was involved in any unlawful activity in regard to the arrest of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Brashich, just to be absolutely clear, there are three motions that would be withdrawn. The Defence request for return to the FRI filed the 21st of October. The Defence request for habeas corpus filed the 15th and 22nd of November, 1999. The first request was filed in 1999, I should say. Then lastly, the request for judicial assistance filed the 2nd of August, 2000. Those are the three requests. That would be withdrawn, the three motions that would be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: The plea bargain agreement does not specifically respond to that question, Your Honour. But the spirit of the agreement and the intent of the agreement should find favour with this Chamber, ultimately, is that those three requests; the repatriation, the habeas corpus and the judicial assistance be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was under the impression it was more than a matter of just the spirit that the agreement was that all three motions would be withdrawn. You seem to be saying that the agreement is that the motion that would be withdrawn is the one related to judicial assistance and in accordance with the spirit of the agreement, the other two would also be withdrawn. That is the motions challenging the legality of the arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Your Honour. What I meant to say, and perhaps I misspoke, is that paragraph 8 does not do so with specificity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It would seem to be sufficiently clear to me because it says here at paragraph 8, "In light of the accused's agreement to plead guilty in accordance with this plea agreement the accused will withdraw all motions pending before the Trial Chamber in which the accused sought an evidentiary hearing regarding the circumstances of his arrest." So that would cover the two motions challenging the legality of his arrest. And then I continue,"... and his request for judicial assistance." So it would seem to me to be quite explicit that it covers all three motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, as this Court is also aware, there are pending certain reviews before the Appeals Chamber. Should the plea agreement not find favour with this Chamber, the Defence reserves its rights under the motions which it has withdrawn as a result of the plea agreement. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will now proceed to address the accused, Mr. Todorovic. Mr. Todorovic, please stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have to ask you some questions to satisfy myself as to the plea that is being made. Mr. Todorovic, you entered into a plea agreement with the Office of the Prosecutor, and pursuant to that agreement, you will plead guilty to the first count of the indictment, persecution, a crime against humanity. Also, in accordance with the agreement, since your plea to count 1 of the indictment encompasses all the allegations in counts 2 to 27, the Prosecutor will accept your plea to count 1 in satisfaction of the remaining 26 counts of the indictment. You will also withdraw all motions pending before the Tribunal challenging the legality of your arrest and seeking judicial assistance. Is that correct? Is that your understanding of the agreement? THE ACCUSED TODOROVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, pursuant to the agreement, the Prosecutor and the Defence will recommend to the Trial Chamber a specific sentence within a range of 5 to 12 years. You must, however, understand that sentence is ultimately a matter for the Trial Chamber to determine in accordance with the Statute and the Rules, and that this may be for a term up to and including life imprisonment. Do you understand that? THE ACCUSED TODOROVIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And have you fully discussed with your counsel the plea agreement that you have entered into with the Office of the Prosecutor? THE ACCUSED TODOROVIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you threatened or coerced in any way to make this agreement? THE ACCUSED TODOROVIC: [Interpretation] No, I was not threatened nor was I coerced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you are entering into this plea voluntarily. THE ACCUSED TODOROVIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And have you discussed the matter fully with your counsel and has he informed you of the nature of the charges against you and of the consequences of pleading guilty to a crime against humanity? THE ACCUSED TODOROVIC: [Interpretation] Yes. My lawyers have fully informed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll now proceed to take the plea. As the indictment is a long one, I want to be sure that we know what the plea relates to. The registrar will take the plea and the specific paragraphs from the indictment, and I'd like both counsel to confirm this. The specific paragraphs that will be read to the accused are paragraph 29, paragraph 30, paragraph 34, and the last two subparagraphs of paragraph 35. Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I concur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar now take the plea?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-9, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Stevan Todorovic, Miroslav Tadic, Simo Zaric, charges Count 1, Persecutions: Beginning in or about September 1991 and continuing through at least 31 December 1993, Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, Stevan Todorovic, and Simo Zaric, together with other Serb civilian and other military officials planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted the planning, preparation, or execution of a crime against humanity, that is, the persecutions of Bosnian Croat, Bosnian Muslim, and other non-Serb civilians on political, racial, or religious grounds throughout the municipalities of Bosanski Samac, Odzak and elsewhere in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The crime of persecutions was perpetrated, executed and carried out by or through the following means: (a) the forcible takeover by Serb forces of cities, towns and villages inhabited by Bosnian Croat, Bosnian Muslim and other non-Serb civilians; (b) the unlawful arrest, detention or confinement of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims and other non-Serb civilians on political, racial or religious grounds and not for their protection and safety; (c) the cruel and inhumane treatment of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims and other non-Serb civilians, including beatings, torture, forced labour assignments and confinement under inhumane conditions; (d) the deportation, forcible transfer and expulsion of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims and other non-Serb civilians from their homes and villages by force, intimidation and coercion; and (e) the wanton and extensive destruction, plundering and looting of the property of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims and other non-Serb civilians, including dwellings, businesses, personal property and livestock. From on or about 17 April 1992 through at least 31st December 1993, Stevan Todorovic, while serving as Chief of Police of Bosanski Samac and as a member of the Serb Crisis Staff, committed and aided and abetted the commission of the crime of persecutions as described in paragraphs 29 and 30 above, through his participation in the following acts or omissions, among others: (a) the forcible takeover of the municipality of Bosanski Samac by Serb forces; (b) the murders, sexual assaults and repeated beatings of numerous Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims and other non-Serb civilians detained in various detention camps in or around the Bosanski Samac municipality; (c) the unlawful detention and confinement of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims and other non-Serb civilians under inhumane conditions on political, racial or religious grounds and not for their protection or safety; (d) the cruel and inhumane treatment of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims and other non-Serb civilians, including beatings, torture, forced labour assignments and confinement under inhumane conditions; (e) the interrogation of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims and other non-Serb civilians who had been arrested and detained, and forcing them to sign false and coerced statements; (f) the deportation, forcible transfer and expulsion of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims and other non-Serb civilians, including women, children and the elderly, from their homes and villages by force, intimidation, and coercion; and (g) the issuance of orders and directives which violated the rights of the Bosnian Croat, Bosnian Muslim and other non-Serb civilians to equal treatment under the law and infringed upon their enjoyment of basic and fundamental rights. By these actions Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, Stevan Todorovic and Simo Zaric planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted the planning, preparation or execution of: Count 1: Persecutions on political, racial and religious grounds, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(h) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Registrar, will you ask how he pleads.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic, how do you plead? THE ACCUSED TODOROVIC: [Interpretation] I plead guilty to count 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit, Mr. Todorovic. You may sit. THE ACCUSED TODOROVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, there is one other matter that I want to raise with you. What does the Prosecution intend to do with counts 2 to 27? Will the Prosecutor be formally withdrawing those counts?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That would be our intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. As I indicated earlier, the second part of this hearing will be for the Trial Chamber to determine whether it is satisfied as to the matters set forth in Rule 62 bis and enter a finding of guilt, if it is so satisfied. The date for that hearing is Friday, the 12th of January, 2001. Prior to that hearing, the parties will submit a brief which will set out the full factual basis for the counts to which the plea relates, including the accused's participation in the crimes, and also attach witness statements. That brief will be submitted by January 5th, 2001. If neither of the parties wish to raise any other matter, the hearing is adjourned. Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just confer with Ms. Paterson for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, after conferring with Ms. Paterson, I don't think there is any other matter that the Defence wishes to raise at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brashich. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
